books.section: Topic 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

options.misconception: Enslavement under the encomienda was the Spanish pattern, not the French one.
options.text: The French enslaved Native peoples to work in mines and missions

options.misconception: Driving Native peoples off the land was the English pattern in Virginia and New England.
options.text: The French drove Native peoples off their land to build settler farms
The French relied on Native allies and trading partners to supply the fur trade

rationales.A: Enslavement under the encomienda was the Spanish pattern, not the French one.
rationales.B: Driving Native peoples off the land was the English pattern in Virginia and New England.
rationales.C: The French came for furs, and furs came from Native hunters, trappers, and guides — the French could not get them any other way. Champlain's 1609 alliance with the Huron was a business partnership as much as a military one, and French traders lived in Native villages, learned Native languages, and married into Native families. The English in Virginia wanted land; the French in Canada wanted partners, because without partners there was no trade.
rationales.D: The French did the opposite of avoiding contact — they lived among Native peoples.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what each power wanted. The English wanted land; the French wanted furs.
2. Ask how furs were got. Only Native hunters, trappers, and guides could supply them.
3. Notice what dependence required. The French had to live among Native peoples, learn their languages, and keep their friendship.
Remember: what a colony wants decides how it treats the people already there.

stem: Compared with the English in Virginia, the French in Canada depended on Native peoples in which of the following ways?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing standard background on the French, the Huron, and the Beaver Wars.
stimulus.text: The French came to North America for beaver fur, and they could not get it without Native partners. Samuel de Champlain allied with the Huron in 1609, and French traders lived among Native peoples, learned their languages, and married into their families. But contact brought disaster: after 1634, measles and smallpox swept the Huron villages, killing between half and two-thirds of their people. Weakened by disease, the Huron were then destroyed in 1649, when some 1,000 Iroquois warriors, armed with Dutch guns and hungry for beaver territory, burned their mission villages and killed about 300 people.
